items.title: Let the Action Mailer test helper load without Active Job
items.body:
Since Action Mailer no longer depends on Active Job (#59820, unreleased), an application can use Action Mailer without the `activejob` gem, but `ActionMailer::TestHelper` still requires it. The railtie includes that helper in every integration test, so such an application raises `LoadError: cannot load such file -- active_job` as soon as `ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest` loads, and every `ActionMailer::TestCase` does too. [Discourse](https://github.com/discourse/discourse/blob/033c474926c78398869d5dd0fbd729f4c3709594/Gemfile#L11-L17) lists the frameworks it uses without Active Job, and its test suite fails this way on Rails main.

This requires Active Job only when it is available and includes its test helper only then. Without it, `capture_emails`, and so `assert_emails` with a block, runs the block directly. The assertions for enqueued emails still need Active Job.

items.title: Bump the minimum supported SQLite version to 3.37.0
items.body:
Since #52354 (Rails 8.0), [`data_source_sql`](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/088fc0cf61e4ba0c7987decafacc69adb3e22eec/activerecord/lib/active_record/connection_adapters/sqlite3/schema_statements.rb#L218-L227) reads `pragma_table_list`, added in SQLite 3.37.0. On main, [`check_version`](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/088fc0cf61e4ba0c7987decafacc69adb3e22eec/activerecord/lib/active_record/connection_adapters/sqlite3_adapter.rb#L518-L522) accepts 3.35.0 after #58284 (unreleased), so SQLite 3.35 and 3.36 fail during uncached schema discovery with `no such table: pragma_table_list`, breaking `bin/rails db:prepare` and model operations that need it.

Raise the connection-time check to 3.37.0 to report the missing requirement clearly. Raw SQL and model operations using a preloaded schema cache can still work on these versions; this change refuses those connections too. Only apps building the `sqlite3` gem against an older system SQLite are affected; the gem bundles a current SQLite.

items.title: Note in the upgrade guide that default_url_options is frozen by default
items.body:
#58483 froze the `default_url_options` Hash that controllers, mailers and every other class including the URL helpers start with. Neither the CHANGELOG nor the upgrade guide mentions it. Code that sets a host in place now raises when the application hasn't configured the options, which showed up in Spree's test suite on Rails main:

```ruby
ActionMailer::Base.default_url_options[:host] = "shop.example.com"
# 8.1:  sets the host
# main: FrozenError: can't modify frozen Hash: {}
```

Callers that fail on Rails main:

* Spree 6.0.6's [`BaseMailer#ensure_default_action_mailer_url_host`](https://github.com/spree/spree/blob/314dcb7784475b3b02ab482ba37882ff100f1365/spree/core/app/mailers/spree/base_mailer.rb#L182), which [`mail` calls](https://github.com/spree/spree/blob/314dcb7784475b3b02ab482ba37882ff100f1365/spree/core/app/mailers/spree/base_mailer.rb#L65) for every email of a store with a storefront URL;
* rails_admin 3.3.1's [`spec_helper.rb`](https://github.com/railsadminteam/rails_admin/blob/ab5ae554288314e406b2e10ece556c342cec40a4/spec/spec_helper.rb#L44), when its suite loads.

This adds a section to "Upgrading from Rails 8.1 to Rails 8.2" with the three replacements (configure the options, assign a new Hash, override the method) and notes that `routes.default_url_options` is unaffected.

items.title: Add missing Active Support core extension requires
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because several files call Active Support core extensions they don't require. In an app, or wherever Action Controller is loaded, something else has loaded the extension first, so the gap is hidden. With only Active Support or Action Dispatch loaded, they raise `NoMethodError`:

```ruby
require "action_dispatch"

ActionDispatch::Static.new(->(env) { [404, {}, []] }, "public")
# static.rb: undefined method 'index_with' for an instance of Array (NoMethodError)

ActionDispatch::ContentSecurityPolicy.new { |p| p.script_src "'self' https://example.com" }.build
# content_security_policy.rb: undefined method 'squish' for an instance of String (NoMethodError)
# (instead of ContentSecurityPolicy::InvalidDirectiveError)

ActionDispatch::SSL.new(->(env) { [200, {}, []] }, ssl_default_redirect_status: 301)
# ssl.rb: undefined method 'squish' for an instance of String (NoMethodError)
# (instead of the deprecation warning)

ActionDispatch::Http::URL.url_for(host: "example.com", path: "/posts", params: { page: 2 })
# url.rb: undefined method 'to_param' for an instance of Integer (NoMethodError)
```

```ruby
require "active_support"
require "active_support/logger"

ActiveSupport::Logger.logger_outputs_to?(Logger.new(STDOUT), STDOUT)
# logger.rb: undefined method 'try' for an instance of Logger::LogDevice (NoMethodError)
# ActiveSupport::CombinedConfiguration#reload fails the same way.
```

### Detail

This Pull Request adds the missing requires, as asked in #59997 (this PR) and #60001:

| File | Require |
|------|---------|
| `action_dispatch/middleware/static.rb` | `active_support/core_ext/enumerable` |
| `action_dispatch/http/content_security_policy.rb` | `active_support/core_ext/string/filters` |
| `action_dispatch/middleware/ssl.rb` | `active_support/core_ext/string/filters` |
| `action_dispatch/http/url.rb` | `active_support/core_ext/object/to_query` |
| `active_support/logger.rb` | `active_support/core_ext/object/try` |
| `active_support/combined_configuration.rb` | `active_support/core_ext/object/try` |

It supersedes #59998, #60000 and #60001.

### Additional information

With the change, each snippet above works: the middleware and logger load, the CSP raises `InvalidDirectiveError`, SSL prints the deprecation warning, and `url_for` returns `http://example.com/posts?page=2`. items.title: Honor DATE_FORMATS overrides of built-in formats
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #59974.

On main, `Time::DATE_FORMATS[:short] = "%-d %b, %H:%M"` no longer changes `to_fs(:short)`. `lookup` returns the frozen built-in as soon as the key exists, so the deprecated hash is only consulted for new names. The same applies to `Date::DATE_FORMATS`. An application that still sets `:short`, `:long`, or `:db` keeps the new built-in text, with only a deprecation warning.

### Detail

`DATE_FORMATS` writes publish the entries that differ from the original built-ins. `lookup` uses that override, unless `register` has replaced the same name, in which case the registered format wins.

The deprecated hash cannot be shared with another Ractor. A shareable snapshot is what other Ractors read. If the override itself cannot be shared, a non-main Ractor keeps the built-in value for that name, and `to_fs` of every other format still works.

Removing a built-in key from `DATE_FORMATS` drops that format again. `Hash#initialize` would otherwise keep the write hook as `default_proc`, and reading the missing key would call the hook again.

`DateTime#to_fs` uses `TimeFormats`, so the same override applies there.

### Additional information

Before, on main:

```ruby
Time.now.to_fs(:short)
# => "26 Nov 22:12"
Time::DATE_FORMATS[:short] = "%-d %b, %H:%M"
Time.now.to_fs(:short)
# => "26 Nov 22:12"
Time.utc(2024, 3, 5, 14, 7).to_fs(:short)
# => "05 Mar 14:07"
```

After:

```ruby
Time.now.to_fs(:short)
# => "26 Nov 22:12"
Time::DATE_FORMATS[:short] = "%-d %b, %H:%M"
Time.now.to_fs(:short)
# => "26 Nov, 22:12"
Time.utc(2024, 3, 5, 14, 7).to_fs(:short)
# => "5 Mar, 14:07"

ActiveSupport::TimeFormats.register(:short, "%H:%M")
Time.utc(2024, 3, 5, 14, 7).to_fs(:short)
# => "14:07"
```

Assigning the deprecated hash still prints the deprecation warning. A non-main Ractor formatted the overridden `:short` as `"5 Mar, 14:07"` and `:db` as `"2024-03-05 14:07:00"`.

Active Support tests, 0 failures: `time_ext_test.rb` 182 runs / 896 assertions, `date_ext_test.rb` 109 runs / 628 assertions, `date_time_ext_test.rb` 124 runs / 448 assertions, and the `to_fs` examples in `time_with_zone_test.rb`.

items.title: Don't run a query when checking `or` compatibility
items.body:
### Motivation / Background This Pull Request has been created because `Relation#or` runs a query while it builds the relation when `from` holds an association relation. The structural compatibility check compares the `from` values with `==`, and `AssociationRelation#==` is `other == records`, so the subquery relation is loaded and thrown away. ```ruby relation = Post.from(author.posts.select(Arel.star), "posts") relation.where(id: 1).or(relation.where(id: 2)) # => SELECT "posts".* FROM "posts" WHERE "posts"."author_id" = ? ``` ### Detail This Pull Request changes `structurally_incompatible_value?` to treat identical value objects as compatible without calling `==`. Both sides of `or` and `and` usually come from the same base relation, so they share the value. `==` already returns true for an identical object, so the result doesn't change; only the query goes away. ### Additional information Two relations whose `from` holds different association relation objects still go through `==` and still load. Avoiding that would mean changing `FromClause#==` or `AssociationRelation#==`, which this PR leaves alone.
Executable test case (fails on main, passes with this change) ```ruby # frozen_string_literal: true require "bundler/inline" gemfile(true) do source "https://rubygems.org" gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main" gem "sqlite3" end require "active_record/railtie" require "minitest/autorun" ENV["DATABASE_URL"] = "sqlite3::memory:" class TestApp < Rails::Application config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f config.eager_load = false config.logger = Logger.new(nil) config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base" end Rails.application.initialize! ActiveRecord::Schema.define do create_table :posts, force: true create_table :comments, force: true do |t| t.integer :post_id t.boolean :flagged end end class Post < ActiveRecord::Base has_many :comments end class Comment < ActiveRecord::Base belongs_to :post end class BugTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase def test_or_with_association_relation_in_from_does_not_load_it post = Post.create! post.comments.create!(flagged: true) base = Comment.unscoped.from(post.comments.select(Comment.arel_table[Arel.star]), "comments") queries = [] callback = ->(*, payload) { queries << payload[:sql] unless payload[:name] == "SCHEMA" } ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribed(callback, "sql.active_record") do base.where(flagged: true).or(base.where(flagged: false)) end assert_empty queries, "Relation#or ran a query while building the relation:\n#{queries.join("\n")}" end end ```

items.title: Fix the `:content_type` description in `register_encoder` docs [ci skip]
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because the documentation of `ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest.register_encoder` describes the `:content_type` option as "The String MIME type of the response body".

`:content_type` is the `Content-Type` of the requests made with that encoder. The built-in `:html` encoder, for example, is registered with `content_type: "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"`:

```ruby
post "/people", params: { name: "David" }, as: :html
request.media_type # => "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"
```

`test_encoding_as_html` asserts this media type.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes the description to say "request body".

### Additional information

The response parser is chosen from the MIME type of the response, whatever `:content_type` the encoder was registered with. With an encoder registered as

```ruby
ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest.register_encoder :csv,
  param_encoder: -> params { "a,b\n" },
  response_parser: -> body { [:parsed_by_csv_encoder, body] },
  content_type: "application/vnd.probe"
```

a request made with `as: :csv` is sent with `Content-Type: application/vnd.probe`. A `text/csv` response is parsed by `response_parser`, and an `application/vnd.probe` response is returned as the raw body.

The option was added in eac1f55425 to set the request header, and the description in 738fa48e64 (#49513).

items.title: Add `change_check_constraint` for PostgreSQL 19+
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

#59796 added the `enforced:` option to `add_check_constraint`, so a check constraint can be created as `NOT ENFORCED`. There is no way to change an existing check constraint between `ENFORCED` and `NOT ENFORCED` without raw SQL.

PostgreSQL 19 allows `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER CONSTRAINT ... [NOT] ENFORCED` for check constraints. This pull request adds `change_check_constraint` for it, as `change_foreign_key` does for foreign keys.

### Detail

- It requires PostgreSQL 19. PostgreSQL 18 supports this statement only for foreign key constraints.
- Changing a constraint to `ENFORCED` checks all existing rows. It raises `ActiveRecord::CheckViolation` if a row violates the constraint, and the constraint stays `NOT ENFORCED`.
- Like `change_foreign_key`, it is not registered in the migration command recorder.

### Additional information

- [PostgreSQL 19.0 Release Notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/19.0/#RELEASE-19-CONSTRAINTS)

  > Allow ALTER TABLE ALTER CONSTRAINT ... [NOT] ENFORCED for CHECK constraints (Jian He)
  >
  > Previously enforcement changes were only supported for foreign key constraints.

- PostgreSQL commit: [Add support for altering CHECK constraint enforceability](https://git.postgresql.org/pg/commitdiff/342051d73b386ad763e13930e15031f7ba5367f5)

items.title: Stop setting the Action Mailer delivery job in `load_defaults`
items.body:
Since #59820 Action Mailer no longer depends on Active Job, and its `delivery_job` reader falls back to `ActionMailer::MailDeliveryJob` on its own. But `load_defaults "6.0"` and later still set `config.action_mailer.delivery_job = "ActionMailer::MailDeliveryJob"`, and the railtie constantizes it when Action Mailer loads. That file requires Active Job, so an app whose Gemfile lists the Rails components with `actionmailer` and without `activejob` raises `LoadError: cannot load such file -- active_job` when a mailer loads, including at boot with eager loading, as I found booting [Discourse](https://github.com/discourse/discourse/blob/d57bed343995d40d7cbe917f5e10b9e695a579fb/Gemfile#L11-L17) on main, even though it never needs Active Job to load a mailer.

This removes the redundant default, so the delivery job, and Active Job with it, is only loaded when something uses it. Apps that bundle Active Job get the same `MailDeliveryJob` as before.

items.title: Look up an existing connection lease without the registry mutex
items.body:
While profiling association loads in a few Rails apps, it turned out that since #59844 `LeaseRegistry#lease` takes a mutex on every call, and with it `lease_connection`, `with_connection` and `active_connection?`. The mutex is needed when a lease is created, so that it gets the terminated flag of the registry that stores it. This returns an existing lease without it; a lookup that misses, as on a thread's or fiber's first call, still creates the lease under the mutex. A concurrent disconnect can still invalidate a returned lease, just as it can immediately after a synchronized lookup.

```ruby
# SQLite in memory; the author has three posts and a profile.
Benchmark.ips do |x|
  x.report("has_one reset/load") { author.association(:profile).reset; author.profile }
end
```

```text
this change
```

items.title: Apply the rest of the scope of a `disable_joins` association
items.body:
`DisableJoinsAssociationScope#add_constraints` only took the conditions and order from the scope of the association, while `AssociationScope` merges the rest of the association's own scope into the query, except `where`, `includes`, `unscope`, and `order`, which it handles by itself. So lazily loading a `disable_joins` association ignored its `select`, `limit`, `includes`, `readonly`, `strict_loading`, and so on.

```ruby
class Author < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :posts
  has_many :latest_comments, -> { order(id: :desc).limit(3) }, through: :posts, source: :comments, disable_joins: true
end

author.latest_comments
# Before: SELECT "comments".* FROM "comments" WHERE ("comments"."post_id" IN (?, ?, ?)) ORDER BY "comments"."id" DESC
# After:  SELECT "comments".* FROM "comments" WHERE ("comments"."post_id" IN (?, ?, ?)) ORDER BY "comments"."id" DESC LIMIT ?
```

Preloading it already applies them, as does loading it without `disable_joins`.

Merge them into the query of the last link, which is the one that loads the records, and add the `includes` there in the same way. When the records of the last link are put in the order of the previous one in Ruby, the values are carried over to that relation too, except the order, `limit`/`offset`, which would cut the records before they are reordered, `select`, which could leave out the key the records are grouped by, and `unscope`, which is already applied and would remove the key conditions.

items.title: Bound quoted-name cache entries by byte size
items.body:

This caps each cached quoted name at 1 KiB. Larger names are still quoted and returned, but bypass caching. The regression test verifies both cache behavior and that quoting still returns the name.

Before this change, a local run quoting two 1 MiB names retained about 4 MiB across their cache keys and quoted values.

Tests: `activerecord/bin/test test/cases/quoting_test.rb` (38 runs, 58 assertions). The available local Ruby is 3.2.3, so a temporary compatibility shim supplied two Ruby 3.3 APIs missing from that runtime during test setup.

items.title: Keep adapter-specific index readers on every `IndexDefinition`
items.body:
#59850 moved `lengths`, `opclasses`, `type`, `include` and `nulls_not_distinct` into `MySQL::IndexDefinition` and `PostgreSQL::IndexDefinition`. `IndexDefinition` is `:nodoc:`, but code that runs on any adapter reads these attributes on whatever `connection.indexes` returns, and on main that raises `NoMethodError`:

```ruby
# PostgreSQL
index = ActiveRecord::Base.lease_connection.indexes(:posts).first
index.lengths # 8.1: {}  main: NoMethodError
index.type    # 8.1: nil main: NoMethodError
```

items.title: Don't share nested values of a column default between records
items.body:
### Problem

```ruby
# t.json :settings, default: { "notifications" => { "email" => true } }
alice = User.new
alice.settings["notifications"]["email"] = false

User.new.settings # => {"notifications"=>{"email"=>false}}
```

Main casts and freezes each column default once (f126797d45), and a new record gets a `dup` of it. The `dup` is shallow, so the nested Hash is the same object for every record: changing it on one record changes the default for every record built after it, and they save it. On 8.1 every record cast its own copy. The same happens with PostgreSQL arrays.

### Fix

A record now gets a `deep_dup` of a frozen default.

items.title: Rescue all Redis errors in RedisCacheStore failsafe
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

`RedisCacheStore` is supposed to be fault tolerant: if Redis errors, a read is a miss, `fetch` computes the value, and the error goes to the `error_handler`. The cache is an optimization, so it shouldn't take pages down.

The store rewritten on redis-client (#57004) only rescues `RedisClient::ConnectionError` in `failsafe`. #57476 had added `RedisClient::Error` to the rescue list, but it was merged the same day as the rewrite and only made it into what is now `DeprecatedRedisCacheStore`.

So any command error now raises from every `Rails.cache` call. Against a real Redis:

| | 8.1.4.1 | main |
|---|---|---|
| Redis full (`maxmemory` + `noeviction`, common when Redis is shared with a job queue): `write` / `fetch` | `nil` / computes the value | `RedisClient::OutOfMemoryError` |
| Wrong password | `nil` | `RedisClient::CommandError` |
| `WRONGTYPE` on read / `fetch` | `nil` / computes the value | `RedisClient::WrongTypeError` |
| `increment` on a key holding a cache entry | `nil` | `RedisClient::CommandError` |

With Redis full, every page that touches the cache would return a 500 instead of just running uncached.

### Detail

Rescue `RedisClient::Error` in `failsafe`, like the previous store.

The existing failure tests only raise connection errors (the "max clients reached" one used to raise a command error with the old store, and now raises `CannotConnectError`), so I added failure safety and failure raising tests that raise `RedisClient::OutOfMemoryError`. The safety ones fail without this change.

No CHANGELOG entry, since the redis-client store isn't released yet.

items.title: Compare scalar ids without arrays in nested attributes
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

`accepts_nested_attributes_for` finds each submitted child by id with a linear scan, twice per child (once in the existing records, once in the association target). So updating N children does about N² id comparisons. That was already the case in 8.1, but each comparison was cheap.

5052ff19f7 (#57638) dropped the single-column branch of `find_record_by_id`, so every comparison now does `Array(record.id).map(&:to_s)`, even for a plain integer id: three objects per comparison instead of one, times N².

`User.find(id).update!(posts_attributes: [...])` with every post sent back with its id, PostgreSQL, YJIT:

| children | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 50 | 463 i/s, 9,968 allocs | 595 i/s, 4,768 allocs |
| 200 | 62 i/s, 129k allocs | 117 i/s, 48k allocs |
| 1000 | 3.3 i/s, 3.0M allocs | 8.0 i/s, 1.0M allocs |

### Detail

Bring back the single-column branch from 8.1, and convert the submitted id to a String once, outside the loop. Composite keys keep the Array comparison.

The lookup is still quadratic. Indexing it with a Hash would help large forms (I measured about +30% more at 200 children), but the association target can change through callbacks in the middle of the loop, so that's a bigger change for another PR.

items.title: Locate an Array of records passed to a job with one query per model
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Pass an Array of records to a job:

```ruby
NotifyJob.perform_later(users) # 100 users
```

When the job runs, Active Job deserializes each Global ID on its own, so you get 100 `SELECT ... WHERE id IN ($1)` queries before `perform` even starts. Global ID already has `Locator.locate_many`, which does one query per model, but Active Job never used it.

On PostgreSQL (local, so no network latency), executing a job with 100 records:

| | queries | i/s | allocations |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 100 | 83 | 11,278 |
| after | 1 | 462 | 4,161 |

With the database on another host, every saved query is also a saved round trip.

### Detail

When every element of an Array is a Global ID, locate them together with `locate_many(gids, ignore_missing: true)`. It keeps the order and does one query per model.

The errors are the same as with `Locator.fetch`:
- a missing record raises `RecordNotFound`, so you get `DeserializationError::RecordNotFound`;
- any other error is wrapped in `RecordUnavailable`, so you get a plain `DeserializationError`.

Arrays whose Global IDs come from more than one app, or don't parse, are located one by one as before.

One visible change: if the same record appears twice in the Array, both positions now get the same instance. Mentioned in the CHANGELOG.

items.title: Reset the dirty tracker before dup copies the record
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

After #59935 (backported to 8-1-stable in #59945), `dup` on a record with optimistic locking can give the copy a `nil` `lock_version`:

```ruby
person = Person.find(1)
person.changed?   # anything that builds the dirty tracker

copy = person.dup
copy.lock_version # => nil   (8.1.4.1: 0)
copy.changes      # => {"lock_version" => [0, nil]}
```

Wait, why would removing an unused include do that? It changed the ancestor order. `ActiveModel::Dirty` now comes before `ActiveRecord::Locking::Optimistic`, so `Dirty#initialize_dup` wraps `Locking#initialize_dup` instead of the other way around. `Locking` then calls `_clear_locking_column` while the copy still holds the original's `@mutations_from_database`. So the change is cleared on the wrong record:

- the copy keeps `nil`, plus a change from 0. The database still gets 0, but the in-memory copy is wrong.
- the original loses a pending `lock_version` change. That's the value you get from the hidden `lock_version` field the locking docs suggest for forms:

```ruby
person.lock_version = 5   # e.g. from params
person.changed?
person.dup
person.lock_version_change # => nil   (8.1.4.1: [0, 5])
```

### Detail

Reset `@mutations_from_database` before `super` in `ActiveModel::Dirty#initialize_dup`, so the copy never uses the original's tracker, whatever the module order is.

No CHANGELOG entry, because #59935 isn't in a release yet. It should go to 8-1-stable too, before the next 8.1 release.

items.title: Give Live actions the event reporter context and tags of their request
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

The `Rails.event` docs say "Context is reset automatically before and after each request". That's not true inside `ActionController::Live` actions.

Context and tags live in Fiber storage, and a new thread copies Fiber storage from the thread that creates it. Live runs actions on a `CachedThreadPool`, so a pool thread is created inside some request and keeps that request's context for as long as it lives. The executor's `clear_context` runs on the request thread, not on the pool thread.

So with the documented pattern:

```ruby
class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  before_action { Rails.event.set_context(user_id: current_user&.id) }
end

class ExportsController < ApplicationController
  include ActionController::Live

  def index
    Rails.event.notify("export.started", for_user: current_user&.id)
    send_stream(filename: "export.csv") { |stream| ... }
  end
end
```

alice hits the export first, then bob, then carol, then someone signed out:

```
export.started payload={for_user: "alice"} context={user_id: "alice"}
export.started payload={for_user: "bob"}   context={user_id: "alice"}
export.started payload={for_user: "carol"} context={user_id: "alice"}
export.started payload={for_user: nil}     context={user_id: "alice"}
```

Rails' own `action_controller.request_started` / `request_completed` events get the same wrong context. If the context is set in a middleware instead, the Live action never sees it.

This is on 8.1 too.

### Detail

`new_controller_thread` runs on the request thread, so capture the context and tags there. On the pool thread, set exactly those with a new `EventReporter#with_context_and_tags` (nodoc), and clear the context when the action is done. It goes through `context_store`, so a custom `event_reporter_context_store` works too.

After this, the same requests give `alice`, `bob`, `carol` and `{}`.

The Live test uses real threads (like the other tests in `LiveStreamTest`) and fails without the change.

items.title: Keep the unaliased table name for left_joins when eager loading
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

Since #59059, when a query has `left_joins` (or `where.missing`) and `eager_load` on the same table, the eager load join takes the plain table name and the `left_joins` join gets the alias. So anything that names the table, like `where(users: ...)`, `pluck("users.name")` or `where.missing`, now hits the eager loaded association instead of the join it was written for. No error, just different rows:

```ruby
class Ticket < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :reporter, class_name: "User"
  belongs_to :assignee, class_name: "User"
end

Ticket.left_joins(:assignee).where(users: { name: "bob" }).eager_load(:reporter)
# 8.1.4.1: tickets assigned to bob
# main:    tickets reported by bob
```

A few more, same data on 8.1.4.1 and main:

| | 8.1.4.1 | main |
|---|---|---|
| `Ticket.left_joins(:assignee).eager_load(:reporter).pluck("tickets.title", "users.name")` | assignee names | reporter names |
| `Post.eager_load(:approved_comments).where.missing(:comments)` | posts with no comments | also posts that have comments |
| `Post.left_joins(:comments).where(comments: { author: "bob" }).eager_load(:comments)` | loads all comments | loads only bob's |

Plain `joins` still behaves like 8.1, so right now `joins` and `left_joins` disagree on which join gets the plain name.

### Detail

The eager load and the `left_joins` dependencies are both rooted at the model, so neither depends on the other. Putting the `left_joins` one first gives back the 8.1 aliases, and both still come before the merged joins that need their tables, which is what #59059 fixed. Its tests in `merging_test.rb` still pass.

The two new tests fail on main without this change.

items.title: Limit the size of the quoted name caches
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

The SQLite3, MySQL and PostgreSQL adapters cache every name passed to `quote_column_name` and `quote_table_name` in process-wide `Concurrent::Map`s (`QUOTED_COLUMN_NAMES` and `QUOTED_TABLE_NAMES`), and never clear them.

Most names come from the schema, so the caches stay small. But hash arguments to `order` and `where` are quoted before the database sees them, and apps commonly build them from params:

```ruby
Post.order(params[:sort] => params[:direction])
```

Each unique `sort` value adds a cache entry, even when the query then fails with an unknown column. With SQLite on main, 1,000 unique names add 1,000 entries to each cache, and 20 calls with a 1 MB name keep about 38 MB of strings alive until the process restarts.

### Detail

Stop caching new names once a cache holds 1,000 entries (the same number as the default statement cache limit). Names that are already cached are still returned from the cache; other names are quoted on every call, which is what happened before they were cached.

The helper lives in `Quoting::ClassMethods`, so the three adapters share it.

The tests fill each cache up to the limit, check that a new name is quoted but not cached, and then remove the names they added.

items.title: Check the encrypted file key length when decrypting
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

`ActiveSupport::EncryptedFile` checks the key length when writing, but not when reading. Because `[key].pack("H*")` pads an odd-length hex string with a `0`, a key that ends in `0` and loses its last character still decrypts the file:

```ruby
key       = "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcde0" # 32 characters
short_key = "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcde"  # 31 characters, dropped last 0

[key].pack("H*") == [short_key].pack("H*") # => true
```

So an app can boot and read its credentials with a shortened key, and `credentials:edit` only fails when saving, after you've made your edits.

This probably doesn't happen in practice, but it's nice to check the key upfront anyway.

### Detail

- Check the key length when reading as well as when writing, so any key of the wrong length raises `InvalidKeyLengthError`. Keys that are too short no longer reach OpenSSL and raise its `ArgumentError`. Comma-separated / rotated keys are now also checked one by one.
- The credentials and encrypted commands print the error and exit 1. `edit` fails before opening the editor.
- `credentials:diff` prints the raw encrypted file, as it already does for `InvalidMessage`, so `git diff` keeps working.

Feel free to discard it if you need to (e.g. when you just fix a typo). -->

### Motivation / Background

A mailer action can choose not to send an email, either by returning without
calling `mail` or by having a `before_action` halt it:

    def welcome(user)
      return unless user.subscribed?
      mail(to: user.email)
    end

In that case Action Mailer replaces the message with a `NullMail`, and nothing
is delivered. However, `deliver_now` and `deliver_now!` still wrapped the no-op
delivery in `run_callbacks(:deliver)`, so `before_deliver`, `around_deliver` and
`after_deliver` all ran as if an email had been sent. Any `after_deliver` that
records a delivery (logging, marking a notification as sent, etc.) records a
send that never happened.

### Detail

- `deliver_now` and `deliver_now!` only run the deliver callbacks when the
  action called `mail`. `deliver_later` is covered as well, because the
  delivery job calls `deliver_now`.
- Adds an internal `ActionMailer::Base#mail_was_called?` (`:nodoc:`) for the
  check.
- Two existing tests used `test_raise_action`, which never builds an email, only
  as "some action other than `test_message`" to test the `only:`/`except:`
  filters. They now use `another_test_message`, so they keep testing the
  filters rather than relying on the old behaviour.

### Additional information

This is a behaviour change for apps that relied on deliver callbacks firing for
emails that weren't sent. That seems unlikely to be intentional, but it's noted
in the CHANGELOG.

items.title: Only draw Action Mailbox conductor routes in local environments
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because the Action Mailbox conductor routes (`/rails/conductor/action_mailbox/*`) are drawn from the engine's `config/routes.rb` in every environment, including production. `Rails::Conductor::BaseController#ensure_development_env` responds with `403 Forbidden` outside of development, so they are not usable there, but:

- they are listed by `bin/rails routes` in production, and
- requests to them reach a controller and get a `403` rather than the `404` any unknown path gets. Security scanners commonly flag this as an exposed admin/debug endpoint.

Other development-only tools are handled differently. `/rails/info` is only prepended in development (`Rails::Application::Finisher`), and `/rails/mailers` only when `config.action_mailer.show_previews` is enabled, which defaults to development. Both are marked `internal: true`, so they stay out of `bin/rails routes` and the routing error page.

### Detail

This Pull Request moves the conductor routes out of `actionmailbox/config/routes.rb` and into an `after_initialize` hook in `ActionMailbox::Engine`, following the `/rails/mailers` pattern:

- They are prepended to the application routes only when `Rails.env.local?`.
- They are marked `internal: true`. `internal:` isn't supported by `resources`, so the `resources :inbound_emails` line is expanded into the four routes it generated. Paths, route names, and order are unchanged, so the existing `main_app.rails_conductor_*` helpers in the conductor controllers and views keep working.
- The test environment keeps the routes. The conductor controller tests draw routes in test and switch to development per request with `with_rails_env("development")`, and applications may do the same.
- The `ensure_development_env` guard in the controller is unchanged.
- The inbound email ingress routes (`/rails/action_mailbox/*`) stay in `config/routes.rb`, since they are meant to be reachable in production.

This also removes the `# TODO: Should these be mounted within the engine only?` comment. Moving the conductor into the engine's own route set would require every app to `mount ActionMailbox::Engine` (a breaking change), and in practice apps would mount it only in development. Following the existing pattern for development-only routes gives that result without the breakage.

Tests:

- `railties/test/application/routing_test.rb` gains "is accessible in development" and "is not accessible in production" tests, matching the `/rails/mailers` ones in `mailer_previews_test.rb`.
- The expected `bin/rails routes` output in `railties/test/commands/routes_test.rb` no longer includes the conductor routes.

### Additional information

I considered a configuration option instead, along the lines of `config.active_storage.draw_routes`. #41687 proposed `config.action_mailbox.draw_routes` and was closed after the suggestion to not load frameworks an app doesn't use. That advice doesn't cover the conductor, which is wanted by apps that do use Action Mailbox, just never outside development. Since the conductor can't be used outside development anyway, an option would only allow drawing routes that always respond with `403`.

items.title: Fix the nested attributes `expect` example in Strong Parameters docs
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because the `accepts_nested_attributes_for` example in the documentation of `ActionController::StrongParameters` filters out every nested record when it is used as written.

`actionpack/lib/action_controller/metal/strong_parameters.rb` documents:

```ruby
class Person
  has_many :pets
  accepts_nested_attributes_for :pets
end

def person_params
  # It's mandatory to specify the nested attributes that should be permitted.
  # If you use `permit` with just the key that points to the nested attributes hash,
  # it will return an empty hash.
  params.expect(person: [ :name, :age, pets_attributes: [ :id, :name, :category ] ])
end
```

`expect` reads a single array as the keys of one hash. The attributes of a `has_many` association arrive as a hash keyed by index (forms) or as an array (JSON), so the declaration above returns no pets, which is the outcome the comment in the example warns about:

```ruby
# pets_attributes: { "0" => { name: "Rex", category: "dog" }, "1" => { id: "7", name: "Tom", category: "cat" } }
params.expect(person: [ :name, :age, pets_attributes: [ :id, :name, :category ] ]).to_h
# => {"name" => "Ann", "age" => "30", "pets_attributes" => {}}

# pets_attributes: [{ name: "Rex", category: "dog" }]
params.expect(person: [ :name, :age, pets_attributes: [ :id, :name, :category ] ]).to_h
# => {"name" => "Ann", "age" => 30}
```

The person is saved, the pets are silently dropped, and nothing raises.

The documentation of `expect` itself says "In order to permit an array of parameters, the array must be defined explicitly. Use double array brackets", and the Form Helpers guide uses that form for the same case (`addresses_attributes: [[ :id, :kind, :street ]]`).

### Detail

This Pull Request changes the example to declare the nested attributes with double array brackets:

```ruby
params.expect(person: [ :name, :age, pets_attributes: [[ :id, :name, :category ]] ])
```

With it, both shapes are permitted:

```ruby
# => {"name" => "Ann", "age" => "30", "pets_attributes" => {"0" => {"name" => "Rex", "category" => "dog"}, "1" => {"id" => "7", "name" => "Tom", "category" => "cat"}}}
# => {"name" => "Ann", "age" => 30, "pets_attributes" => [{"name" => "Rex", "category" => "dog"}]}
```

`parameters_expect_test.rb` already asserts the array shape for double brackets (`"key to explicit array: returns permitted array"`). It had no test for nested attributes keyed by index, so this PR adds one that asserts the value shown above.

The single array has been in the example since it was converted from `require(:person).permit(...)` in e1d58cfd05.

### Additional information

items.title: Treat a missing namespaced class as a MessagePack cache miss too
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

#59683 made a MessagePack cache entry whose class no longer exists a cache miss. That only holds for a top-level class. When the class is namespaced, the missing constant is the last part of its name (`Billing::Invoice` without `Invoice`) or one of its namespaces (`Billing` itself is gone), and the entry raises `NameError` instead of being treated as a missing class:

```ruby
dumped = ActiveSupport::MessagePack::CacheSerializer.dump(Billing::Invoice.new)
# ... Billing::Invoice is renamed or removed ...
ActiveSupport::MessagePack::CacheSerializer.load(dumped)
# top-level class: ActiveSupport::Cache::DeserializationError: Missing class: Invoice
# namespaced:      NameError: uninitialized constant Billing::Invoice
```

What this means for a cache store with `serializer: :message_pack`:

| | missing top-level class | missing namespaced class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| main | cache miss | cache miss, but the error reported is the `NameError` |
| 8-1-stable (has the backport of #59683) | cache miss | `read`, `exist?`, `read_multi` and `fetch` raise `NameError` |

On 8-1-stable this is what a rolling deploy runs into: a release starts caching a new namespaced model with `Rails.cache.fetch`, and the instances still running the previous release raise on that key; or a model is renamed and the old entries raise until they expire. Most application classes are namespaced.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes the MessagePack class loading so that a `NameError` counts as a missing class when the missing constant is any part of the class name, the same rule `ActiveSupport::Inflector#safe_constantize` applies. A `NameError` for an unrelated constant, raised while the class is being loaded, is still raised as is.

A test next to the existing one for a top-level class covers both shapes (the class is missing, the namespace is missing); it fails without the change.

No CHANGELOG entry, like #59683.

### Additional information

Follow-up to #59683. I had proposed the namespaced case in #58084, before #59683, and closed it when it went stale. Since #59683 is in `8-1-stable`, this may be worth backporting there as well; that is where the `NameError` reaches the application. Output of a `MemoryStore` with `serializer: :message_pack` on the tip of `8-1-stable` (3d1b2cf4aa):

```

fetch("top") { :recomputed }             :recomputed
read("namespaced")                       RAISED NameError: uninitialized constant Billing::Invoice
exist?("namespaced")                     RAISED NameError: uninitialized constant Billing::Invoice
read_multi("namespaced")                 RAISED NameError: uninitialized constant Billing::Invoice
fetch("namespaced") { :recomputed }      RAISED NameError: uninitialized constant Billing::Invoice
```

items.title: Fix `Response` raising when the Content-Type header is not a String
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because, on main, a response whose Content-Type header is set to something that is not a String, such as a `Mime::Type`, raises `NoMethodError` when the media type or the charset is read, and when the response is committed. 8.1 reads such a value like the string it converts to.

```ruby
response.headers["Content-Type"] = Mime[:json]

response.media_type
# 8.1:  "application/json"
# main: NoMethodError: undefined method '-@' for an instance of Mime::Type

response.to_a # committing the response
# 8.1:  returns the status, headers and body
# main: NoMethodError: undefined method '-@' for an instance of Mime::Type
```

A controller that sets the header this way and then renders or sets `response_body` returns a 500 on main. Applications do this; for example blackcandy's `StreamController` sets `response.headers["Content-Type"] = Mime[@stream.format]` before streaming a file (`app/controllers/stream_controller.rb` in blackcandy-org/blackcandy). It has worked so far because the server converts the value when it writes the header.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes `ActionDispatch::Response` so that a Content-Type header value that is not a String is parsed on each read, as it was before the parsed header was memoized in #59096 and #58966. String values are memoized as they are now.

items.title: Fix preloading ordered `has_many :through` scoped on its through table
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because, on main, preloading a through association whose scope has a hash condition on the through table loses the order of the scope when the order is given as a Symbol, a Hash or an Arel attribute. 8.1 keeps the order.

```ruby
class Author < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :categorizations
  has_many :special_categories,
    -> { where(categorizations: { special: true }).order(:name) },
    through: :categorizations, source: :category
end

author.special_categories.map(&:name)
# => ["Cooking", "General", "Technology"]

Author.preload(:special_categories).find(author.id).special_categories.map(&:name)
# 8.1:  ["Cooking", "General", "Technology"]
# main: ["General", "Cooking", "Technology"]
```

Two more shapes of the same problem:

- A scope that also has a hash condition on the source table, such as `where(categorizations: { special: true }).where.not(name: "General").order(:name)`, raises `ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` when preloaded (`no such column: categories.name` on SQLite3, `missing FROM-clause entry for table "categories"` on PostgreSQL). It works on 8.1.
- A `has_one :through` with such a scope returns another record than when it is loaded lazily, because the order that picks the record is not applied.

`includes` behaves like `preload`. The order written as an SQL string (`order("categories.name")`) is not affected.

### Detail

The through query applies the conditions and the order of the scope, so the source table has to be joined in it. This Pull Request joins the source table whenever the scope has conditions, as it already is when the conditions are given as an SQL string.

Until 63cf73e451 (not in a release), an order on the scope's own table counted as a reference to the source table, which is what made these scopes join it. A scope with hash conditions on both tables and no order had no such reference and raised before that commit too (it does on 8.1); it is fixed as well.

One visible change for scopes that already worked: a scope with hash conditions on the through table only (`-> { where(categorizations: { special: true }) }`) is now loaded with that join as well, instead of a separate query for the source records. The loaded records are the same. If keeping two queries for that shape is preferred, the join can be limited to scopes that have an order or conditions on the source table; I'm happy to change it.

No CHANGELOG entry, since the regression is not in a release.

### Additional information

Two tests are added to `eager_test.rb`. Without the change the first one fails (wrong order) and the second one errors (`StatementInvalid`).

To check that nothing else moves, I compared lazy loading with `preload` for a matrix of 107 scoped through associations (conditions on the through table, the source table or both, combined with `order`, `reorder`, `or`, `not`, `rewhere`, `distinct`, `group`, `limit`, `includes`, `preload`, `annotate`, `lock`, `extending`):

| | lazy and preload agree | disagree |
| --- | --- | --- |
| main | 50 | 57 |
| this PR | 74 | 33 |

All 24 changes are from "disagree" to "agree"; none goes the other way. Five of them agree on 8.1.4.1 (the regression) and the other 19 disagree there as well. Of the remaining 33, 32 also disagree on 8.1.4.1 and are long-standing differences this change does not touch; the last one (a `rewhere` of a condition that comes from the source association) differs between 8.1.4.1 and main for a reason unrelated to this change.

The comparison gives the same numbers on SQLite3 and on PostgreSQL 17. On PostgreSQL, 27 of the preloads that raise on main no longer do, and no preload or lazy load raises only with this change.

Tests run: `bin/test test/cases/associations test/cases/associations_test.rb test/cases/relation test/cases/relations_test.rb test/cases/strict_loading_test.rb test/cases/scoping` on SQLite3 (3149 runs, 0 failures) and on PostgreSQL 17 (3185 runs, 0 failures), plus the whole suite with `rake test:postgresql` (11349 runs, 0 failures, 0 errors). items.title: Fix `order(Arel.sql(...).desc)` making `includes` load with a join
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because, on main, ordering by an SQL literal with a direction extracts a table reference from the literal. Whatever comes before the first dot of the literal is taken as a table name, so `includes` switches from preloading to a join. 8.1 does not extract a reference from this form.

```ruby
Post.includes(:comments).order(Arel.sql("1.0 * posts.tags_count").desc)
# 8.1:  references_values => [], comments are preloaded
# main: references_values => ["1"], comments are loaded with a LEFT OUTER JOIN,
#       and `count` becomes COUNT(DISTINCT "posts"."id") over that join

Comment.includes(:commentable)
  .joins("INNER JOIN users u ON u.id = comments.user_id")
  .order(Arel.sql("u.name").asc)
# 8.1:  the polymorphic association is preloaded
# main: ActiveRecord::EagerLoadPolymorphicError
```

A column that exists on both tables also becomes ambiguous once the association is joined (`Post.includes(:comments).order(Arel.sql("1.0 * position").asc)` raises `ambiguous column name: position` on SQLite3 and `PG::AmbiguousColumn` on PostgreSQL).

### Detail

This Pull Request changes the references extracted from `order`, `reorder` and `default_order` so that an ordering counts as a reference only when it wraps an attribute, as in 8.1. This is also the scope the message of 63cf73e451 gives for the extraction: "`Arel::Attribute` (or its `Ordering`) and `String`".

An SQL string given to `order`, such as `order("comments.body DESC")` or `order(Arel.sql("comments.body DESC"))`, is still scanned for a table name.

The literal of an ordering is scanned since 63cf73e451, which is not in a release, so there is no CHANGELOG entry.

### Additional information

`references_values` for each way of writing the order, with `Post` as the model:

| `Post.order(...)` | 8.1.4.1 | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `"comments.body DESC"` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` |
| `Arel.sql("comments.body DESC")` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` |
| `Arel.sql("comments.body").desc` | `[]` | `["comments"]` | `[]` |
| `Arel.sql("1.0 * posts.id").desc` | `[]` | `["1"]` | `[]` |
| `Arel.sql("comments.body") => :desc` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` | `[]` |
| `"comments.body" => :desc` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` |
| `:"comments.body"` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` |
| `comments: { body: :desc }` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` |
| `Comment.arel_table[:body].desc` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` |
| `Comment.arel_table[:body] => :desc` | `[]` | `["comments"]` | `["comments"]` |
| `Arel.sql("comments.body").desc.nulls_last` | `[]` | `[]` | `[]` |

One form still differs from 8.1: an SQL literal used as a hash key (`order(Arel.sql("comments.body") => :desc)`). It is built into the same node as `Arel.sql("comments.body").desc`, so the two cannot be told apart once the references are extracted from the built nodes, and this PR treats them the same way. If keeping the reference for the hash key form is preferred, it would have to be carried separately from the nodes; I'm happy to do that here instead.

Tests: `bin/test test/cases/relation test/cases/relations_test.rb test/cases/associations/eager_test.rb test/cases/associations/has_many_through_associations_test.rb test/cases/calculations_test.rb test/cases/batches_test.rb test/cases/scoping` on SQLite3 (2011 runs, 0 failures) and on PostgreSQL 17 (2045 runs, 0 failures), plus the whole suite with `rake test:postgresql` (11349 runs, 0 failures, 0 errors). items.title: Fix `ConnectionPoolFiberTest` leaking a connection from pool maintenance
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because `activerecord trilogy (yjit)` timed out in the nightly CI. After one `ConnectionPoolFiberTest` test reported a leaked connection, every test took 20 seconds or more.

https://buildkite.com/rails/rails-nightly/builds/4943#01a1fac2-84d8-4102-b039-2de9ccb5a143

```
ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::ConnectionPoolFiberTest#test_reap_removes_connection_when_reset_fails = Found 1 leaked connections
owner: #<Thread:0x00007f5285433cb0@ActiveRecord-global-async-query-executor-worker-4 (snip) dead>
(snip)
20.56 s = E
ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::ConnectionPoolFiberTest#test_disconnect_terminates_existing_leases = 20.05 s = .
```

### Detail

This Pull Request changes `ConnectionPoolFiberTest` to change the isolation level only while no pool maintenance is in progress.

`ConnectionPoolFiberTest` changes `ActiveSupport::IsolatedExecutionState.isolation_level` to `:fiber` in `setup` and restores it in `teardown`. The isolation level is process wide, and maintenance of the other connection pools may be running on an async executor thread at that time.

Pool maintenance leases a connection, works on it and expires it. `lease` records `ActiveSupport::IsolatedExecutionState.context` as the owner, and `expire` raises unless the owner is the current context. When the isolation level changes in between, the owner and the current context are the thread and its fiber, or the other way around:

```
ActiveRecord::ActiveRecordError: Cannot expire connection, it is owned by a different thread
```

The connection stays in use and `@maintaining` is never decremented. `check_connection_leaks` then reports "Found 1 leaked connections", and in every later test it waits five seconds for each pool, until the job times out.

Pool maintenance on the async executor was added in #54175. The five second wait is `wait_for_pool_maintenance`, which #57744 added to `check_connection_leaks`.

### Additional information

The leak can be reproduced by changing the isolation level while pool maintenance has a connection:

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "cases/helper"

class IsolationSnippetTest < ActiveRecord::TestCase
  self.use_transactional_tests = false

  def test_isolation_level_change_during_maintenance
    pool = ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool
    pool.with_connection { |conn| conn.select_value("SELECT 1") }
    pool.release_connection

    started = Concurrent::Event.new
    resume = Concurrent::Event.new
    pool.send(:sequential_maintenance, ->(conn) { true }) do |conn|
      started.set
      resume.wait(5)
    end
    assert started.wait(5)

    previous = ActiveSupport::IsolatedExecutionState.isolation_level
    ActiveSupport::IsolatedExecutionState.isolation_level = :fiber
    resume.set
    sleep 0.5
    ActiveSupport::IsolatedExecutionState.isolation_level = previous

    assert_empty pool.connections.select(&:in_use?)
  end
end
```

```
Found 1 leaked connections
owner: #<Thread:0x00007f5739bc7bf8@ActiveRecord-global-async-query-executor-worker-1 (snip)>
(snip)
Failure:
IsolationSnippetTest#test_isolation_level_change_during_maintenance:
Expected [#<ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::TrilogyAdapter:0x000000000020d0 env_name="arunit" role=:writing>] to be empty.
```

`ConnectionPoolFiberTest` with a thread that keeps running `pool.reaper_lock { pool.keep_alive(0); pool.preconnect }` on every pool of `ConnectionPool::Reaper.pools`, as the reaper does, every 2 milliseconds:

| | Adapter | Seed | Leak reports | "Cannot expire connection" errors | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Before | trilogy | 1 | 1 | 1 | 352 seconds |
| Before | trilogy | 2 | 2 | 2 | 428 seconds |
| After | trilogy | 1 | 0 | 0 | 2 seconds |
| After | trilogy | 2 | 0 | 0 | 2 seconds |
| After | trilogy | 3 | 0 | 0 | 2 seconds |
| After | sqlite3 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 second |
| After | postgresql | 1 | 0 | 0 | 2 seconds |

With this thread `test_keepalive_notices_problems` still fails after this change, because the thread repairs the connection that the test breaks on purpose.

This Pull Request does not handle maintenance that takes more than five seconds. `wait_for_pool_maintenance` gives up after five seconds, and the isolation level is changed anyway.

items.title: [memory ⬇️] CodeGenerate class_attribute methods
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because `class_attribute` compiles its readers, writers and predicates with a `class_eval` on every call, so every class that declares an attribute gets its own copy of the same instruction sequences. Attribute names repeat across an application: a concern declares the same attributes on every class that includes it. In a large application, 2,466 `class_attribute` calls compiled only 227 distinct sources.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes `class_attribute` to define its methods with `ActiveSupport::CodeGenerator`, as attribute methods and (since #59393) association methods already are, so classes that declare the same attribute share one compiled copy.

- The generated code depends only on the attribute name, whether it has an instance reader (baked into the writer), and whether it's declared on a singleton class (the instance reader differs). Each combination gets its own namespace.
- Class methods are still defined before instance methods. `CurrentAttributes.method_added` relies on that order; an earlier version that defined instance methods first made it generate a delegating class method, which the class reader then redefined.
- `attr_writer` still runs in the owner after the generated methods, as before.

### Additional information

- Measured in a large application after boot and a full GC, this saves ~8 MB of retained memory.
- The Active Support suite has the same results as `main` locally, apart from environment-dependent file watcher, CI-runner timing and backtrace cleaner tests that fail with and without this change. No new warnings appear under `-w`. The Active Model and Active Record (sqlite3) suites pass.
- The added tests cover the cases sharing could get wrong: the same attribute name declared with and without an instance reader, and on a class and a singleton class.

items.title: Don't drop the STI type condition when joining
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because, since 3adff4f636 (#59823), joining or eager loading an STI subclass association loses the STI type condition when the association scope has its own condition on the inheritance column:

```ruby
class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :special_comments_except_sub, -> { where.not(type: "SubSpecialComment") }, class_name: "SpecialComment"
end

post.special_comments_except_sub                       # SpecialComment records only, as expected
Post.joins(:special_comments_except_sub)               # also matches Comment and VerySpecialComment rows
Post.eager_load(:special_comments_except_sub).find(id) # raises ActiveRecord::SubclassNotFound
```

```sql
INNER JOIN "comments" ON "comments"."deleted_at" IS NULL
  AND "comments"."type" != 'SubSpecialComment'
  AND "comments"."post_id" = "posts"."id"
```

The type condition is now added in `klass_join_scope`, before `join_scope` merges the association scope on top of it, and merging a `WhereClause` drops existing predicates on attributes the merged scope also uses. Before that commit the type condition was added after the merge, so it was kept. This only affects `main`.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes `Reflection#join_scope` to add the type condition back after merging the association scope when the merge removed it, the same way `keep_owner_conditions` re-applies the owner conditions. Loading the association keeps the type condition, so joining now matches it. When the type condition survives the merge nothing changes, so the SQL of other STI joins stays the same.

items.title: Don't compare owner conditions when joining an association without a scope
items.body:
Since #59836, `join_scope` compares the where clauses before and after merging the association's scope items, to
detect owner conditions the scope removed. It does so also when there are no scope items. Comparing predicates can
call into their bind values: `Array#-` hashes both sides once they are large enough, and `QueryAttribute#hash` and
`#==` serialize the value. So joining an association whose target default scope has an out-of-range condition
raises `ActiveModel::RangeError` instead of matching no records:

```ruby
class Child < ActiveRecord::Base
  default_scope { where((0..16).to_h { |i| [:"key#{i}", 1] }.merge(key0: 2**70)) }
end

class Parent < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :children
end

Parent.joins(:children).to_a # => ActiveModel::RangeError (Rails 8.1: [])
```

This skips the comparison when there are no scope items, since nothing can have removed a condition.

items.title: Return no messages for an attribute when a model has no errors
items.body:
Form builder fields call `errors[method]` to decide whether to wrap the field in `field_error_proc`, and views often ask `errors[attr]` the same way. On a model without errors, `messages_for` still normalized the attribute and type, filtered the empty error list and mapped the result: three Arrays and two Hashes for an empty result.

It now returns an empty Array right away when there are no errors.

```ruby
require "active_support/all"
require "active_model"
require "benchmark/ips"

class Post
  include ActiveModel::Model
  attr_accessor :title
  validates :title, presence: true
end

post = Post.new(title: "Hello")
post.valid?

Benchmark.ips do |x|
  x.report("errors[:title]") { post.errors[:title] }
  x.report("errors[\"title\"]") { post.errors["title"] }
end
```

```
ruby 4.0.7 (2026-09-15 revision 229531a6cf) +YJIT +PRISM [x86_64-linux]

before:      errors[:title]      4.776M (± 1.2%) i/s  (209.37 ns/i) -     24.214M in   5.069759s
before:     errors["title"]      3.639M (± 4.8%) i/s  (274.80 ns/i) -     18.541M in   5.095148s
after:       errors[:title]     18.933M (±10.0%) i/s   (52.82 ns/i) -     95.088M in   5.022489s
```

items.title: Keep readonly when preloading a filtered through
items.body:
Preloading a `readonly` `has_many :through` with conditions returns records that are not readonly, while loading the same association lazily returns readonly records:

```ruby
class Author < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :posts
  has_many :readonly_welcome_post_comments, -> { where("posts.title = 'Welcome to the weblog'").readonly }, through: :posts, source: :comments
end

Author.first.readonly_welcome_post_comments.first.readonly?
#=> true
Author.preload(:readonly_welcome_post_comments).first.readonly_welcome_post_comments.first.readonly?
#=> false
```

For a `has_many :through` with conditions, the preloader loads the through records with one query that eager loads the source records, so the conditions can reference the through table. `JoinDependency` builds the source records with the scope of the source association, which has no `readonly`, and the preloader reuses the source records unchanged.

### Changes

`ThroughAssociation#records_by_owner` now marks the source records readonly when the scope of the through association is readonly. Preloading a readonly `has_many :through` whose source is a `has_many :through` with conditions now returns readonly records too.

items.title: Skip copying form field names that need no changes
items.body:
Form builder fields such as `text_field` and `checkbox` compute their id with `field_id` and their name with `field_name`, and `Tags::Base#sanitized_method_name` strips a trailing `?` from the method name. For usual names such as `post` and `title`, none of them changes anything, but each made a copy: `field_id` copied the object name twice and the method name once, `field_name` joined an empty Array into a new String, and `sanitized_method_name` copied the method name.

This makes each copy only when there is something to replace. A `_` counts as nothing to replace, because `field_id`'s `gsub` turns it into itself. Ids and names are the same as before.

```ruby
require "active_support/all"
require "active_model"
require "action_view"

class Post
  include ActiveModel::Model
  include ActiveModel::Attributes
  attribute :title, :string
  attribute :published, :boolean
end

view = ActionView::Base.empty
form = ActionView::Helpers::FormBuilder.new(:post, Post.new(title: "Hello", published: true), view, {})

{ "text_field" => -> { form.text_field(:title) }, "checkbox" => -> { form.checkbox(:published) } }.each do |name, field|
  field.call
  before = GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects)
  1000.times { field.call }
  puts "#{name}: #{(GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects) - before) / 1000} objects"
end
```

```
ruby 4.0.7 (2026-09-15 revision 229531a6cf) +PRISM [x86_64-linux]

before: text_field: 28 objects
before: checkbox: 32 objects
after:  text_field: 22 objects
after:  checkbox: 26 objects
```

Under Callgrind, a `text_field` call runs about 3% fewer instructions in the interpreter and 5% fewer with YJIT, and a `checkbox` call about 2% and 4% fewer.

items.title: Unpin the main pool the Ractor proxy pinned
items.body:
While going through two months of Buildkite failures on main, I found that `AsynchronousQueriesTest#test_async_query_retries_connection_failure` fails in the sqlite3:ractor job for some seeds. On unpin, the Ractor connection proxy looked the main pool up again by name, role and pool token and unpinned nothing, so the writing pool stayed pinned for later tests. The proxy now unpins the main pool it pinned, as `ConnectionPool` itself does. The commit explains the cause.

Run together with the two tests that set it up, in random order, the async test failed in 15 of 120 runs before and in none after.

items.title: Compare Server-Timing durations with the events they come from
items.body:
While going through two months of Buildkite failures on main, and on pull requests whose failing job had nothing to do with their change, I found that the nested and sibling event tests in `ServerTimingTest` keep turning builds red. Each failure costs a contributor a rerun and a reviewer a look at a failure their change didn't cause.

The tests compared the header with `sleep` lengths under fixed tolerances, so a busy machine failed them. They now compare it with the events it comes from. On two CPUs shared with four busy processes, they failed in 189 of 200 runs before and in none after.

items.title: Skip merging a blank relation into a relation without conditions
items.body:
`Association#target_scope` merges `klass.scope_for_association` into every association scope it builds: every
`has_many` chain (`post.comments.where(...)`, `.exists?`, `.count`), every association reader, and once per
model in a through chain. For a model without a default scope that isn't an STI subclass, that relation is blank,
and the association relation it is merged into has no conditions yet. Merging it adds nothing, but the `Merger`
still goes through every value and merges the where and having clauses, which allocates 5 to 6 objects each time.
In Fizzy, Lobsters, Mastodon and Campfire, that is 39 to 48 percent of the merges in a request.

This returns early when the other relation has no values and the receiver has no where or having conditions. A null
relation still goes through the merge, since it can be null without values (`Post.none.only(:order)`), and so
does a receiver with conditions, because the merge drops duplicate predicates.

```ruby
require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"
  gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"
  gem "sqlite3"
  gem "benchmark-ips"
end

require "active_record"
require "benchmark/ips"

ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:")
ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts
  create_table :comments do |t|
    t.references :post
    t.boolean :approved, default: true
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :comments
end

class Comment < ActiveRecord::Base
  belongs_to :post
end

post = Post.create!
3.times { post.comments.create! }

Benchmark.ips do |x|
  x.report("post.comments.where(approved: true)") { post.comments.where(approved: true) }
end
```

```
ruby 4.0.9 (2026-10-23 revision 3e93b23afc) +YJIT +PRISM [x86_64-linux]

before: post.comments.where(approved: true)    123.359k (± 1.8%) i/s    (8.11 μs/i) -    620.776k in   5.032258s
after:  post.comments.where(approved: true)    141.771k (± 3.4%) i/s    (7.05 μs/i) -    710.696k in   5.012994s
```

Building the chain allocates 32 objects before and 27 after. In full requests of Fizzy, Lobsters and Campfire,
it is 50 to 177 fewer objects and 0.6 to 1.4 percent fewer instructions. With
[#59212](https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/59212), an association reader served by the statement cache would no
longer build its scope; this still covers collection chains, counts and readers that skip the cache.

items.title: Allocate less per field in `text_field_tag` and `tag`
items.body:
Follow-up to #50312. Since `button_to` is built on `form_tag`, each param goes through `hidden_field_tag(name, value, id: nil)` and `text_field_tag`, which computed an id with `sanitize_to_id` only for `id: nil` to drop it.

`text_field_tag` now computes the id only when none is given, so `button_to` keeps calling `hidden_field_tag`. The shared helpers also avoid two intermediate strings: `sanitize_to_id` replaces characters in its first copy instead of making a second, and `tag` freezes its string before `html_safe`, as `content_tag_string` and `self_closing_tag_string` already do.

The output is the same for every name that rendered before. Since the unused id is no longer computed, a name it can't convert, such as one with invalid UTF-8, now renders when an `id` is given instead of raising.

```ruby
require "active_support/all"
require "action_view"
require "benchmark/ips"

ActionView::Helpers::NavigationHelper.button_to_generates_button_tag = true
ActionView::Base.remove_hidden_field_autocomplete = true

view = ActionView::Base.empty
one = { "key" => "value" }
two = { "key" => "value", "other" => "value" }

Benchmark.ips do |x|
  x.report("button_to, 1 param") { view.button_to("Save", "/posts", params: one) }
  x.report("button_to, 2 params") { view.button_to("Save", "/posts", params: two) }
end
```

```
ruby 4.0.7 (2026-09-15 revision 229531a6cf) +YJIT +PRISM [x86_64-linux]

before:   button_to, 1 param     56.620k (± 5.4%) i/s   (17.66 μs/i) -    286.092k in   5.052861s
before:  button_to, 2 params     42.216k (± 5.0%) i/s   (23.69 μs/i) -    213.920k in   5.067315s
after:    button_to, 1 param     60.368k (± 4.3%) i/s   (16.57 μs/i) -    302.150k in   5.005115s
after:   button_to, 2 params     45.771k (± 4.4%) i/s   (21.85 μs/i) -    234.171k in   5.116144s
```

A `button_to` call allocates 3 fewer objects with one param (46 → 43) and 6 fewer with two (63 → 57), and `hidden_field_tag` and `text_field_tag` 2 fewer each. Without params, `button_to` is unchanged.

items.title: Avoid rebuilding attribute names in `LazyIndexedAttributeSet#keys`
items.body:
In #59141, `LazyIndexedAttributeSet#row_keys` became every name in the set's indexes, which already cover every typed attribute of the model. #59833 removed `cached_names` from the union in `#keys`, and the `@ctx.type_keys` left in it adds nothing either: `row_keys | @ctx.type_keys` always equals `row_keys`, but still builds another array, and for more than 16 names a hash, on every call. Dirty tracking and `attribute_names` call `#keys` on every `changed?`, `save`, `inspect` and `serializable_hash`. `materialize`, which `save` and `dup` run, likewise walked the type keys a second time.

This drops the union and the second walk, and with them the context's unused `type_keys`. `#keys` returns the same names in the same order, as `#to_hash` already assumes.

Callgrind instructions and objects per call, Ruby 4.0.9, no JIT, a 30-column record:

| | main | this change |
|---|---:|---:|
| `changed?` | 191,805 (3 objects) | 166,885 (1) |
| `serializable_hash` | 203,514 (35) | 178,220 (33) |
| `update!` of one column | 1,375,929 (189) | 1,301,611 (183) |
| `find` then `save` | 1,530,171 (169) | 1,402,222 (163) |
| `find` then `dup` | 1,118,770 (182) | 1,062,870 (182) |

items.title: Add enforced option to add_check_constraint on PostgreSQL 18+
items.body:
### Motivation / Background

PostgreSQL 18 adds `NOT ENFORCED` to CHECK constraints. Rails supports `enforced:` for foreign keys only.

### Detail

This Pull Request adds `enforced:` to `add_check_constraint` and `t.check_constraint` on PostgreSQL 18+. `check_constraints` reads it back, and the schema dumper writes it.

### Additional information

Other adapters ignore `enforced:`, as they do for `add_foreign_key`. MySQL 8 also supports `CHECK ... NOT ENFORCED`. Should that go in this PR or in a follow-up?

* [x] This Pull Request is related to one change. Unrelated changes should be opened in separate PRs.
* [x] Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If this PR fixes a related issue include it in the commit message.
